column1: How the architecture is numbered, and what each layer, mode and step means.

column3: Meaning
A process area, numbered 01 to 19. Each L1 carries one decision or serves all of them.
A sub-process inside one L1, numbered L1.n, for example 7.3.
A process inside one L2, numbered with the L1 as two digits, for example 07.3.1. The items under an L2 are always called L3 processes.
The case moves through these processes in order. 01 to 05 run on EFS before day 90; 06 to 10 run on the Workbench.
Run across every core process when they are needed.
Set the rules every process runs by, and read the results.
Runs at every decision point in every core process.
A rule, engine or agent completes the step. No person is involved; the result is in the log.
An agent or engine prepares, recommends or drafts. A person decides, approves or completes.
A bank employee carries out the step. The Workbench prepares the task and records the result.
A physical or legal act done outside any system, such as a title transfer. The Workbench records that it happened.
A partner carries out the step: an agency, law firm, valuer, auction house, broker or court officer.
Gather and check the facts the decision needs.
Apply a rule, a model or an agent to choose an option.
Make the choice final, or route it to the person with the authority to approve it.
Carry out the choice in the Workbench, another system or through a partner.
Record the decision, the action and the result once, in the decision log.
The nine decisions a case passes through: act on the signal, reach the customer, promise kept, escalate, offer a restructure, which route, next legal step, how to dispose, write off or pursue.
The seven deviations that interrupt a decision: dispute or complaint, vulnerable customer or hardship, deceased customer, fraud, bankruptcy or external seizure, lost contact, collateral event.
